title: Twenty Planners, Ten Doers, One Researcher

callouts.label: Task Queue
callouts.hint: Find the pile of cream paper stacks resting at the far left end of the belt, where the belt begins.
callouts.description: The ordered list of tasks waiting to be done, with their status, kept as a plain file in the project so the agents and the researcher read the same record. Each task in the breakdown has an owner role, an input, an output, and an acceptance check.

callouts.label: Handoff Card
callouts.hint: Find the plain cream tile with a document-lines icon, the last unlit one on the belt before the glowing run, with an orange arrow pointing right from it.
callouts.description: A handoff carries the goal, inputs, constraints, acceptance criteria, work done, and open questions in one agreed format and place. A minimal protocol uses five statuses: queued, running, needs-review, accepted, rejected. An agent never marks its own work accepted.
callouts.tip: A handoff is where information is lost, so design it on purpose.

callouts.label: Planning Agent Bank
callouts.hint: Find the two upper rows of small teal figures at little desks, each beside a framed sheet with a map, outline, or checklist.
callouts.description: About twenty planning agents explore, decompose, and specify: surveys, approaches, specifications, and acceptance criteria. Their output is cheap and reversible, so many plans can run in parallel and you choose among them. The 20-to-10 ratio is a design target, not a law.
callouts.tip: A wrong plan costs minutes of reading. A wrong execution costs a rerun.

callouts.label: Review Checkpoint
callouts.hint: Find the low gold arch over the belt with a green check on top, a green glow inside, and a green bar-chart tile passing through; no figure stands beside it.
callouts.description: A defined point where output is examined before the next step uses it. A checkpoint can be automated, such as a test suite or a check script, or run by a reviewer agent. It does not spend your attention. A reviewer agent complements tests and your own sampling, and does not replace them.

callouts.label: Human Approval Gate
callouts.hint: Find the tall maroon-and-gold tower straddling the belt, with an icon of a person holding a pen on its front.
callouts.description: A checkpoint where a person must say yes before work continues. Gates consume the scarce resource, so they belong where actions are irreversible or outward-bound. Reviewing a sample of the cheapest, most reversible outputs is one way to save attention.
callouts.tip: A gate that nobody reads is a gate in name only.

callouts.label: Attention Meter
callouts.hint: Find the big curved gauge at the far right edge, with a dial running from green to red and a needle swung into the red zone.
callouts.description: Researcher attention is the binding limit. In Chapter 10's illustration, 20 planners at 6 minutes, 10 executors at 15 minutes, and 30 minutes of conflicts need 300 minutes against 4 hours of attention. Reviewing half the planning outputs brings the load to 240 minutes.

callouts.label: Execution Agent Bank
callouts.hint: Find the bottom row of dark blue workers with tool belts at benches; look at the second one from the left, facing a monitor with a network of connected circles.
callouts.description: About ten execution agents carry out specified tasks: code, analyses, simulations, figures, and text. Their output changes files and uses resources, and it costs more attention to check, so this side is kept smaller. Give each its own output directory or branch.

callouts.label: Shared Workspace
callouts.hint: Find the long green counter in the middle of the stage, topped with green seated figures, folders, a chart tile, a plant, and book stacks at each end.
callouts.description: The common area where the team's files live. To prevent collisions, give each agent its own output directory or Git branch, keep inputs read-only, and make merging an explicit step that goes through review instead of letting agents write straight into the main line.

callouts.label: Critical Path
callouts.hint: Find the glowing amber run of four tiles joined by arrows on the belt, and look at the mountain-icon tile, second in the run.
callouts.description: Dependencies set what can run in parallel. In Chapter 10's illustrative example, 21 hours of work still takes 18 hours, the longest chain of dependent tasks. More agents cannot shorten it. Only shortening a task on that chain can, and then the next-longest chain takes over.

callouts.label: Status Board
callouts.hint: Find the small standing signboard left of the gold platform, with three rows of colored lights (red, yellow, green) beside short lines.
callouts.description: A short report from the queue and the logs answers four questions: what finished, what is blocked and why, what needs your decision, and what has been spent. Ask an orchestrating agent to produce it each morning, and read it before you read anything else.

callouts.label: The Orchestrator
callouts.hint: Find the maroon-robed figure with a raised baton, standing on the round gold platform at the bottom center, with the border collie beside it.
callouts.description: The orchestrator decides what is done, by which agent, in what order, with what checks, and what happens when something fails. In this book that is the researcher. An orchestrating agent may keep the queue and draft status reports, but the researcher stays accountable.

callouts.label: Conflict Flag
callouts.hint: Find the small red pennant stuck into papers on the green counter, between two green figures right of center.
callouts.description: Two agents produced incompatible results. Do not average them. Decide whether the dispute is about facts or judgment. For facts, trace each result to its inputs and find the first point of divergence, often a different window function or file version. Record the decision and the reason.
callouts.tip: Ask each agent to list inputs, settings, and file versions, then compare line by line.
